newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bunds ride high on EMU mood, but seen vulnerable.
newsitem.headline: Bunds ride high on EMU mood, but seen vulnerable.

text.p: German debt prices remained in positive ground in late trade, boosted by generally EMU-positive sentiment after Europan Union ministers said they had reached a deal on a stability pact and a resolution for jobs and growth.
Although the market dipped back just after the agreement was announced, traders said this could be put down to slight profit-taking on a 'buy the rumour, sell the fact' basis.
By 1427 GMT, the September DTB Bund future was 12 basis points up on the day at 101.66 having reached a high at 101.85 in early business.
In the cash market, the 10-year benchmark Bund was quoted at 102.38 for a 5.675 percent bid yield by the same time.
But while analysts said Bunds looked healthy for now, they warned prices were vulnerable to a set back in the near term.

"In the very short term I would still be relatively bullish, but things are starting to look a bit toppish and a bit overbought," said Jim Dodgin, analyst at Technical Data in London. "The momentum is not really following through."
After the September future reached its 101.85 peak, the market had failed to sustain highs, suggesting that 101.85 to 102.00 would probably act as a ceiling in coming sessions.
"Things are likely to start running out of steam soon and then the 101.85 to 102.00 area is likely to prove pretty hard work to overcome," Dodgin said.
EMU sentiment too, should not be overplayed in terms of pushing Bund yields lower, analysts said.

While the budget pact agreement on Monday would help confidence, some said the market should not forget that the agreement was likely to have been softened slightly by the addition of a resolution on jobs and growth.
France and Germany, who were divided on the issue before the summit, both now say they are happy with the deal.

Analysts said, however, that credibility in the whole EMU project had anyway been damaged significantly by German and French squabbling over the past few weeks, and warned that this may have long-term implications for the monetary policy of the future European Central Bank.

"In their enthusiasm about the chances of EMU starting in 1999 being raised by an Amsterdam compromise, European markets have overlooked that the ECB will ... be relatively independent from politicians' wishes and that the more disregard for stability there is among governments, the tighter monetary policy will have to be," MMS said in a research note.
"Bunds should keep that risk in mind if yields are falling due to EMU enthusiasm in other European countries."
